## Aether Map: a sketch profile is a surface; display diagnosis — 2026-09-13

**The model was wrong and Jonathan's question fixed it.** Masks had been
separate "keep" regions drawn onto a selected surface, so shapes drawn beside
a surface clipped it to nothing and it vanished — his screenshot showed exactly
that. Now **a closed sketch profile is a surface**, the way a closed sketch is
a feature in CAD. Its bounding box is the warp quad (a perspective warp is a
homography, and a homography has exactly four corners — that is the one thing
that must be a quad) and the profile is the outline that clips the picture.
A rectangle is its own quad and carries no outline; an ellipse, polygon, pen
or freehand profile keeps its shape while its four bounding corners warp the
picture. Drawing needs no selection. Round handles warp; square handles move
the outline, and only for outlines of sixteen points or fewer — nobody nudges
an ellipse's forty-eight by hand; it is redrawn instead.

**Cutout** is a latched mode on the Sketch group: the next profiles are
surfaces filled black. A projector masks by projecting nothing, so a black
surface above the picture *is* the mask — no subtractive geometry, and the
existing layer order already says what is on top. Properties' "Masks" section
became "Outline": reset to the quad, start one from the quad, add a point.
The document keeps `masks: Point[][]` unchanged; older files with several
shapes still union them.

**Display listing, diagnosed.** The picker had said "This browser cannot list
displays" with no reason. It now distinguishes an insecure page, an embedding
frame, and a browser without the Window Management API, and names the fix
for each; a failed scan shows the browser's own error text. Jonathan saw one
display of two because his browser is not Chromium: a probe through Chrome on
the same Mac listed both — "BenQ EX3501R 3440×1440 (primary)" and "DELL
SE2422H 1280×720" — so in Chrome, Edge, Arc or Brave the picker lists them,
defaults to the one the editor is not on, matches the raster to it, and opens
the output window there. In any browser, an output window that has been
dragged to the projector and made fullscreen reports its real resolution back,
and both pickers now show that with a Match button — the fallback that works
everywhere.

**Two test bugs found and fixed while proving this.** The end-to-end "Hide
surface" step matched the Layers panel's "Hide Surface 2" eye toggle first, so
the earlier run had passed without ever exercising the cue; it now matches
exactly and tests the cue. And the display e2e granted the permission on
Chrome's default browser context, which Playwright's pages never use; granting
on the right context makes the scan succeed headless.

Validation: 147 aether-map unit tests, 3 end-to-end tests in the installed
Chrome (the show flow now sketches an ellipse that becomes a second surface
clipped to its outline on the projector; the display test lists displays with
the permission granted, matches the raster and reads it back in Properties),
109 host, 177 UI, ruff, oxlint, the theme guard, TypeScript and every build.

Not claimed: placing the output window onto a *second* physical display was
not exercised — headless has one screen, and the headed probe only listed
them. That is the thing only Jonathan's desk can prove.
## Aether Map: sketch tools for masks, colour fills, display picker — 2026-09-13

**Sketch tools.** Masks are drawn the way a CAD sketch is, from a Sketch group on
the ribbon: Select, Pen (click-click, close on the first point, double-click or
Enter to finish, Esc to abandon), Rectangle, Ellipse, Polygon and Freehand, with
single-key shortcuts V/P/M/E/G/N that never fire while typing in a field. A
surface can carry several mask shapes; their union clips it, so a window and a
door are two shapes rather than one awkward polygon. One shape is a CSS
`clip-path`; two or more become an SVG `<clipPath>` union in user space,
identically in the editor and on the projector. Freehand strokes are simplified
with Ramer–Douglas–Peucker; ellipses are 48-gons, indistinguishable from a curve
at projection distance; a tap that never became a drag is discarded rather than
saved as a zero-area mask. The document keeps `masks: Point[][]`; version-2
files that wrote a single `mask` migrate on read.

The glyphs are the illustrated 32×32 tool set Aether CAD uses, through the
shared `ToolIcon`: `rectangle`, `ellipse`, `polygon` and `select` reused;
`pen`, `freehand`, `mask` and `fill` drawn new in the same palette and
registered in `core/ui/src/ToolIcon.tsx` per its README. A "Node" tool was cut
from the plan because it would have done exactly what Select does.

**Colour fill.** A surface can be a solid colour instead of media or text — most
of projection mapping is lighting an edge or a frame — rendered as the same
warped, clipped element.

**Display picker.** Devices now asks *Monitor* or *Edge device*, Monitor being
the default because it is the output that exists today. Chrome's Window
Management API lists every attached display after a permission prompt, with
size and position; the picker defaults to the display the editor is *not* on,
shows whether the raster matches it, offers one-click Match, and opens the
output window placed and sized on that display, where one double-click makes
it fullscreen on the projector. It rescans when a cable comes or goes. Other
browsers only know the editor's own display, and the window is dragged across
by hand — the picker says so. The Output dialog uses the same picker.

**Under the tests.** jsdom has no `PointerEvent`, so testing-library dispatched
bare events with no `button`; a small polyfill gives them the real shape so the
canvas's guards are exercised rather than bypassed. Key handlers now tolerate a
non-Element target instead of assuming one.

## Map: an Add Shape sheet, and the two solids it was missing — 2026-09-19

Measured against the reference's add sheet, Map already had most of it under
different names: Square is the rect tool, Circle the ellipse, Outline the pen,
Text a feature kind, Mapping Background the setup image, and Transparent PNG an
ordinary media import. Two were genuinely absent, and so was the sheet.

**Cube and Box.** Neither is a single plane, which is why neither existed: a
physical box seen from a corner shows three faces that warp independently but
belong together, and a recess shows four walls around a back. Each now builds
its faces and puts them in a folder — grouping already existed, and it is what
makes them move, hide and reorder as one object. Cube is three faces laid out
isometrically so the starting shape reads as a solid; Box is a back panel inside
four walls, which is what an alcove or a window reveal actually presents and
what the reference's icon draws. Nothing here is a 3D engine: they are a
starting arrangement closer than four separate rectangles, and the operator
drags the corners onto the real thing.

**The sheet.** The ribbon already carried every one of these, but it is
organised for someone who knows the tool. The sheet is organised for the moment
you are facing a wall deciding what to put on it: primitives first, then the two
ways of bringing in something you already have, then the automatic ones. It
opens from the surfaces tray's add button.

Picking a primitive arms its drawing tool rather than dropping a shape in the
middle of the scene, because you place a circle by drawing it where it goes.
Cube and Box do drop, because there is nothing to draw.

**Smart tools are shown and disabled.** Smart Shape Detection and AI Generation
are both on the roadmap and both the first thing someone looks for after using
the reference. A row that says "Soon" is more honest than a gap that looks like
nobody considered it, and the disabled rows stay legible rather than fading out,
because they are carrying information.

`shape-groups.test.ts` pins the face count, the folder, distinct ids, that no
face is degenerate, that every corner lands inside the scene, that a portrait
scene gets a shape sized to it, and that a compound shape saves as a contiguous
grouped run. `add-shape.spec.ts` drives the sheet: every entry present and
enabled, the two smart rows disabled, a cube arriving as one folder of three
with three strip cells, a box adding five more in its own folder, and a
primitive arming its tool instead of dropping a shape.

## Map: the surfaces tray, and the tray each room opens on — 2026-09-19

**Mapping opens on the surfaces bar.** The tray always started on the timeline
whichever room you were in. It now opens on the tray that answers that room's
question — surfaces in Mapping ("which shape is that one?"), timeline in
Sequence ("when?") — and remembers your choice *per room*, the way the ribbon
tab beside it already does, so picking the timeline while mapping survives a
trip through Sequence and back.

Writing that turned up a bug in my own first attempt: the reader listed three of
the five tray ids, so choosing Export or Audio was silently discarded and fell
back to the default. `WorkspaceID` is now derived from an exported
`WORKSPACE_IDS`, and the reader checks against that rather than a copy of it.

**The strip is minimal, and stops rearranging itself.** Three things, all on
Jonathan's reference:

*No empty-state layout.* An empty scene swapped the row for a centred panel with
its own heading and button, so the tray changed shape the moment the last
surface went. A tray that rearranges itself cannot be learned. The row is simply
empty now, with the add button where it always is.

*One border per tile.* Each cell drew its own edge and then the thumbnail drew
the scene bounds just inside it — a border around a border. The bounds rect is
gone; the cell's edge is the only one. Captions are gone too, leaving a compact
square tile, with the name on hover and in the accessible label. Selection is
the accent edge alone, without the extra dot that needed explaining.

*An accent add button*, pinned right, instead of a plain icon button.

**Four tokens that never existed.** The strip's CSS referenced
`--aether-color-bg-field`, `--aether-color-text-secondary`,
`--aether-color-bg-canvas` and `--aether-radius-panel`. None are defined, so
those declarations were doing nothing at all — the cells had no fill and no
radius. Replaced with real tokens. The theme-literal guard catches raw colours
but not misspelt variables, which is how these survived.

Six more uses of `--aether-color-text-secondary` and one of
`--aether-color-text-primary` remain in `Aether CAD/src/react/shapr-shell.css`,
already on that guard's known-pending list. Another lane's file; noted, not
touched.

Both the other lane's `surfaces.spec.ts` and the new tray test were updated to
the new intent: an empty scene is an empty row with the add button still there,
and the cell has no inner bounds rectangle.

## Map: the input preview stopped turning itself back on — 2026-09-19

Switching the input preview off did not stick. Nothing was setting it back on —
it was never remembered. `showInput` was plain `useState(true)`, while the
layout preset and the timeline height beside it are both persisted, so every
page load restored it. Map reloads after a save and after a rename, so it came
back every few minutes, which reads as the editor overruling you rather than as
a missing preference.

It is stored under `aether-map.input-preview`, following the pattern the two
settings next to it already use. `layout.spec.ts` covers off-then-reload,
off-then-save (a save reloads too), and back-on-then-reload, because a
preference that only remembers one of its two states is still broken.

**Left alone deliberately:** `snapping` and `xray` in `SurfaceCanvas` are also
unremembered `useState`. They are canvas modes rather than panel visibility and
arguably should start fresh each session, so changing them was not part of this
and wants asking first.

`aether-default` moved from a blue accent on neutral slate to an indigo accent

## Map: the pattern switch was being clipped — 2026-09-19

A `SettingsRow` sizes its control column for a field. A three-option segmented

## Map: the Surfaces pane matches its reference — 2026-09-19

**Defaults.** A plane now starts as a violet checkerboard on screen with a white
edge and white pins, and a black-and-white checkerboard on the projector. Two
near shades rather than one flat colour on screen, because a checker reads as a
*surface* against a photographed wall where a flat fill reads as a hole, and its
squares show a warp the moment a corner moves. Black and white outside, because
maximum contrast is the whole job in a dark room and a checker's corners are
easier to line up against a physical edge than a grid's lines.

**One panel, not two.** The pane showed both sides stacked, which is twice as
much to read for a comparison nobody makes. It is one card now with a
full-width Device / External switch, the way the reference does it — you tune
one side against its own preview and swap.

**The preview** is square, centred in a panel the full width of the pane, drawn
by `SurfaceGrid` itself so what you are choosing cannot drift from what the wall
gets. Pins are drawn *proud of* its corners rather than inside them, which is
where they sit on the canvas, so the pin-size slider shows the thing it changes.
Opacity reads as a percentage rather than a fraction.

One test needed correcting rather than the code: the proportional-stroke test
had been relying on grid being the default, so changing the default broke it. It
asks for a grid explicitly now — it is about line weight and should never have
cared which pattern happened to be default.

271 unit tests, both surface-look e2e specs, lint, `tsc -b`, the theme-literal
guard and the Map build pass.

## Map: a projector sets itself up from a phone — 2026-09-20

**The first step needed a network the device did not have.** Provisioning was
`curl <host>/api/map/install.sh | bash`, which assumes the Pi is already on
Wi-Fi, already knows the host, and has a keyboard and a terminal. A Pi out of
the box has none of those, so the turnkey path could not start.

**A downloadable, self-contained installer.** Devices → Set up a new device now
offers `aether-projector-setup.sh`: the daemon and the wizard base64'd inside
one shell script, built by `core/host/map_provisioning.py`. Copy it to the Pi,
run it, reboot — no network required on the device. Base64 rather than
heredocs because Python source is full of quotes and backslashes, and an
installer truncated by one of them would still run. A test asserts the
embedded modules match the files on disk, parse as Python, and that the whole
thing is valid `bash -n`. The piped one-liner still works for a Pi already on
the network and skips the wizard.

**A first-boot wizard, answered from a phone.** A projector has no keyboard, so
with no network the player raises its own access point and the projector screen
displays what to join and where to go. The wizard asks, in order: Wi-Fi (live
scan, with a refused passphrase reported rather than swallowed), the host
address (`studio.local:8780` accepted as typed), the device name, and three
device permissions. The order is not cosmetic — without a network there is no
host to reach, and without a host there is no name to register.

Joining the chosen network takes the setup access point down and drops the
phone that asked, so the answer is saved before the radio is touched.

**Two faults caught while building it, both about the device on the wall.**
Permissions parsed absent keys as their defaults, so a partial payload could
switch on something nobody ticked; absent now means not granted. More
seriously, the first draft returned the Wi-Fi step for *any* disconnected
device — which would have pulled a running projector off its show and put up a
setup screen the moment a router rebooted, destroying the offline playback
this product exists for. Setup completion is now permanent, a configured
device never raises the access point, and a device provisioned before the
wizard existed is adopted on its next start instead of being marched through
it.

**The permissions are real settings**, not a consent screen: `kiosk.sh` reads
them at launch and disables screen blanking or mutes Chromium to match.

**What is tested, and what cannot be.** 32 Python tests cover the step order,
the nmcli command building and terse-output parsing (including an SSID
containing a colon, and the device's own access point not reading as being
online), the refusals, and adoption. 9 more cover the installer builder,
including the host serving it over HTTP. 2 e2e tests drive the whole wizard in
a browser against the **real** player handler with only the radio faked, and
check the projector screen. **The nmcli conversation itself is unverified** —
joining a network, raising the access point and the captive-portal redirect
need a real Pi with a real wireless card, and nothing here can stand in for
one.

**Not done, and worth saying plainly:** audio and video playback settings
beyond the device-level mute permission. There is no volume, no per-clip audio
and no playback-quality control in the show model at all — `MapShow` has never
had a volume field. That is a separate piece of work from onboarding.

## Map: deploying to a Raspberry Pi was broken, and now runs on a schedule — 2026-09-19

**Every current show silently failed to deploy to a Pi.** `aether_player.py`
gated on `layout.get("version") not in (1, 2)`; the document format moved to 3.
A deploy fetched the show, rejected it as "unsupported layout" to a log nobody
reads, exited 0, and left the projector on its previous picture. `player.spec`
had been failing on exactly this and was being counted as a known-flaky test.
The daemon now reads `SUPPORTED_LAYOUT_VERSIONS`, and a test parses
`show-file.ts` and fails if the two ever disagree again — verified by flipping
it back and watching the test catch it. The renderer that actually draws the
show migrates 1 and 2 forward, so this gate was only ever a sanity check and
must never be narrower than that parser.

**An edge device can now hold a showtime.** `ShowOutput.schedule` is a start
minute, an end minute and optional days; outside its hours the output is dark.

Only an edge device is offered one (Jonathan, 2026-09-20, narrowing where this
first shipped): it is the only output handed a project and left alone. A
monitor or a Cast window lives as long as the machine driving it is awake, and
whoever opened it is present to start the show. Switching an output away from
"Edge device" clears its schedule rather than leaving a rule the panel no
longer shows, quietly blacking out a window. The check itself is
still general, in `showForOutput` — the one place every renderer already asks
what an output shows — so out of hours gives the same answer as unbound, in the editor
preview, the browser output window and the Pi alike, with no renderer needing
to know about time. The output window re-arms a timer on each minute boundary
rather than polling, so showtime starts on the minute.

Local time on whatever draws the picture, deliberately: a projector runs "dusk
to eleven" in its own timezone, and the laptop that programmed it may be
elsewhere or long gone. A window whose end precedes its start runs through
midnight and belongs to the day it opened — a Friday 22:00–02:00 show is still
Friday's show at half past twelve, and that case has a test.

The schedule rides inside the saved show, which is exactly what the host
base64s to a device, so a Pi keeps its hours offline through reboots. Nothing
in the deploy path needed changing.

**Two bugs found by its own tests.** The day toggles showed all seven pressed
when `days` was absent but treated that as an empty selection, so the first
click meant "Mondays only" instead of "all but Monday". And `readOutput` is a
whitelist parser: the schedule set correctly, showed on the row, and vanished
on save and reopen until `readSchedule` was added — validated, not trusted, so
a bad file cannot talk a projector into a nonsense window and leave it dark on
the night.

**One show, several projectors, now actually works.** The kiosk opened
`index.html?output=1` with no output id, so every Pi drew `outputs[0]` and the
`deviceId` binding on outputs 2..N did nothing — a second device projected the
first one's scene. `/player-status` now reports the output whose `deviceId`
matches this device and the portal passes it to the renderer, falling back to
the first output for a device no output names.

**Wireless is as complete as the web allows**, and this is worth writing down
because it looks like a gap. A page cannot start an AirPlay or Cast session on
its own; the operator picks the receiver in the browser or OS. So a Cast output
opens a normal tab, where Chrome keeps its Cast menu, and an AirPlay output
opens a window to share or drag onto an extended display. The transport is
stored on the output and the window reports the size it is actually presenting
at, which is what the crop needs.

11 unit tests cover the schedule rule, its clock parsing and its file
round-trip; 3 e2e tests cover dark-outside-hours against the real clock,
persistence across save and reload, and the through-midnight wording. 9 Python
tests cover the player, including the version-drift guard and per-device output
selection.

## Map: an artboard says what is editing it and what is projecting it — 2026-09-19

**The outline was faint and uneven, and the cause was the zoom.** Everything
inside `.map-artboards` is drawn through the canvas transform, so the old
`box-shadow: 0 0 0 1px` was 1px × zoom on screen. At a normal working scale —
measured at 0.283 on a fresh show — that is a quarter of a device pixel, which
renders as partial alpha, and opposite edges land on different subpixel offsets
and so come out at different weights. That is exactly the "hard to see and not
consistent on all 4 sides" complaint, and the same class of defect as the
surface grid stroke fixed two days ago.

`.map-artboards` now carries its zoom as `--map-zoom`, and every ring is
declared `calc(2px / var(--map-zoom, 1))`. Verified in the browser: at zoom
0.283 the spread computes to 7.07px in artboard space, which is 2.00px on
screen, identical on all four edges. An e2e test zooms out and asserts the
on-screen weight holds.

**An artboard now also shows what is projecting it.** A ring in
`--aether-color-ok` — the colour the tray light already uses for "connected" —
means this scene's picture is going out right now, and a badge beside the
scene name reads `Output 1 · Output window`, naming the output and the device
it plays on. Editing and projecting are different facts, so a scene that is
both carries both rings: accent on the edge, output ring just outside it.

**Only "live" gets a ring, deliberately.** Every new show already aims its one
output at its one scene, so ringing "aimed" as well would put a permanent
border on the default document and tell an operator nothing. The assignment is
on the badge; the ring means on air. An output bound to a scene with its window
closed shows the badge with a dim dot and no ring, and closing a window drops
the artboard from live back to aimed rather than to nothing — the aim survives
the projector.

**Liveness is not a second opinion.** The canvas reuses `outputConnection`,
the same rule the Outputs tree and the Output panel use, through a new
`sceneOutputs` helper in `output-connection.ts`. `KIND_LABEL` moved there as
`OUTPUT_KIND_LABEL` with an `outputDeviceName` helper, so the tree and the
badge cannot drift into different words for the same four kinds.

**`useMapDevices` is now one poll for the app.** Its comment claimed "one hook
so the Outputs tree and the device manager agree", but it held `useState` per
mount: the three existing consumers each ran their own request every ten
seconds and could disagree between ticks. Adding the canvas as a fourth was
what surfaced it. It is a module store now, with one timer that runs while
anything is subscribed and stops when nothing is.

Five unit tests cover `sceneOutputs` and `outputDeviceName`, including that an
edge output is live only while its player is playing *this* show. Three e2e
tests cover the badge, the ring's three states, and the ring weight.

**Worth knowing for anyone running the suite:** `e2e/host.py` serves the built
bundle, and nothing in `playwright.config.ts` builds it. Run `npm run build`
first or the suite tests whatever was built last — half of this change appeared
to be missing until I noticed the served JS had my new attribute but not my new
markup.

## Map: the e2e suite's inconsistency was two runs sharing one checkout — 2026-09-19

**Root cause found, and it was never in the product.** Two Playwright runs in
this checkout — the two lanes, or a rerun launched over a live run — collided
on two shared resources. Every "different failures every run" result quoted in
earlier entries, including the run that died at test 4 with
`ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:8790`, came from this.

*One hardcoded port.* `playwright.config.ts` pinned `PORT = 8790` with
`reuseExistingServer: false`, so a second run tore down the first run's host
mid-test. Measured directly: a single serial run of mine saw **five different
host PIDs** (1852, 5291, 6765, 7168, 17911) while Playwright starts `webServer`
exactly once. The host was not crashing — it was being replaced. Tests that had
passed a second earlier then read `ECONNREFUSED`, and `lsof` still showed a
process LISTENing, which is what made the earlier stale-port theory look right.

*One output directory.* Playwright empties `outputDir` as a run starts, so the
second run deleted the traces the first was still writing. That surfaces as
`ENOENT ... .playwright-artifacts-N/traces/*.network`, not as a test result.

**Both fixed** in `aether-map/playwright.config.ts`: the port is now
`Number(process.env.AETHER_E2E_PORT) || 8790 + (process.pid % 1000)`, written
back into `process.env` so the worker processes — which re-load the config in
their own processes and would otherwise each compute a different number —
inherit it; `outputDir` is `test-results/${PORT}`. `AETHER_E2E_PORT` still wins
when set, so a run can be pinned to a known port.

**Verified.** Two deliberately overlapping runs took ports 9620 and 8935 and
reported **0 refusals each**; the same overlap before the change produced
refusals in the run that was already healthy. `artboards.spec.ts:75` and the
tray specs, previously "failing", pass.

**Theories tested and eliminated**, recorded so nobody re-runs them: stray
background kill-loops of mine (no such processes existed); a full listen
backlog (`request_queue_size` is 5, but 100 concurrent connections against the
host produced zero refusals); file-descriptor exhaustion (`ulimit -n` is
1048576). The earlier entry blaming stale hosts holding 8790 was not the cause
— killing stale listeners helped only because it sometimes removed one of the
two competing runs.

**A blind spot worth knowing.** `webServer` sets no `stdout`/`stderr`, so
Playwright defaults both to `ignore` and any host traceback is invisible. Piping
them via a throwaway config is what made the host's own output readable, and it
showed the host healthy throughout — `BrokenPipeError` on client disconnects
only.

**The suite today, serially, is 66 of 73.** The seven are genuine and are not
infrastructure: `.map-raster` now matching two elements in `artboards`, a
`.map-surface` count inverted in both `authoring` and `scenes`, a missing exact
"Hide" cue button in `show` (fails 3/3 in isolation), a missing "Timeline
playback" combobox in `video`, an Outputs treeitem now reading
`Output 1 Connected · 1280 × 720 · AirPlay · Scene 1 · 1280 × 720` where
`wireless` expects `Active scene · 1280 × 720`, and `player` receiving a bare
`http://127.0.0.1:<random>/` where it expects `index.html?output=1`. These look
like UI-contract drift from today's 47 changed files across both lanes, not one
defect. `player` fails identically with the port pinned to 8790, so the config
change is not implicated; `wireless` passes alone and so is order-dependent.
Attribution is not possible from git — `aether-map/` is entirely untracked, a
single `??` entry, so the product has no history to diff against.

## Map: how a plane looks, set for the screen and the wall separately — 2026-09-18

A Surfaces pane in Map's settings window now controls how a plane with no
content is drawn — and controls it **twice**, once for the editor and once for
the projector.

**This is a deliberate exception to a rule set two days ago.** Everywhere else
the viewport must render exactly what the projector renders, and that still
holds for content. An empty plane is different: on screen you are manipulating
it, so it wants corner pins and enough translucency to see the setup photo
underneath; on the wall you are judging the mapping against a real contour in a
dark room, so it wants hard contrast and no pins, because nothing pins a wall.
The two sides are answering different questions, so they get different answers.
Content still cannot diverge.

**The model.** `SurfaceLook` is `{ device, external }`, each a
`SurfaceAppearance`: pattern (fill, grid or checkerboard), primary and secondary
colours, border, section count, opacity, and — device only — pin size, which
drives the actual corner handle radius rather than being a label. It supersedes
`output.surfacePattern`, which was this idea with one pattern and one side; a
show saved with that carries its choice into both sides on read, so reopening
one looks the way it was left rather than snapping to a default.

Both sides live in the document rather than a browser preference, for the reason
the old setting did: a paired Pi has no access to a preference and its
projection has to look the way the show says. `emptyShow` seeds a copy, not the
shared constant, so editing one show cannot reach through into the default every
other show starts from.

**The pane** uses the shared macOS-style `SettingsWindow`, with Surfaces beside
Workspace in its sidebar. Each side is a card carrying a live preview drawn by
`SurfaceGrid` itself — the same component the wall gets — so what you are
choosing and what you will see cannot drift apart. Colour labels follow the
pattern, because the same slot means "fill and grid line" under one and
"primary and secondary" under another.

**One shared-UI fix found on the way:** `SettingsWindow` marked its current pane
with a CSS class and nothing else, so which pane you were on was not announced
at all. It carries `aria-current="page"` now.

`surface-look.spec.ts` drives the real pane: it gives the editor a fill and the
projector a checkerboard and checks both windows at the same instant, sets a
colour and reads it back off the projected element, reloads to prove the look is
the show's and not the browser's, changes the section count and counts the
resulting lines, and restores one side's defaults without touching the other.

271 unit tests, 198 shared UI tests, lint, `tsc -b`, the theme-literal guard and
the Map and UI builds pass.

## Map: an output is one row, not a folder — 2026-09-17

The Outputs tree gave every output three child rows — its device, its scene, its
region — which read as a hierarchy that is not there. They were attributes in the
costume of items: none could be selected, opened, renamed, deleted or moved, and
a row that answers nothing is not an item in a tree.

An output is one row now. Its **kind is its icon** — a window for a monitor, the
hardware mark for a paired player, a link for cast and AirPlay — because what
kind of thing an output is is the one fact you want before clicking it. The rest
moved to the Output panel, where every other property of a selected thing
already lives, and is also gathered into the row's status tooltip so it can be
read without opening anything.

The status label leads with the connection state, because that is what its icon
means; the device, scene and region follow. Getting that order wrong broke
`show.spec.ts`, which asserts the row announces itself as connected — a good
assertion catching a real regression in what the row says about itself.

`performance-pipeline.spec.ts` now pins the shape: two outputs are two treeitems
with no disclosure control anywhere in the tree, and the device type, scene and
crop controls are all present in the Output panel.

**On the test numbers.** 270 unit tests, typecheck and lint are clean. The e2e
suite reported a *different* three failures on each of several full runs, every
one of which passes in isolation — including `wireless.spec.ts`, which another
lane added at 11:40 today while a run was in flight. Two causes, both
environmental: stale `e2e/host.py` processes holding port 8790 between runs, and
spec files appearing mid-run. The full-suite number is therefore not quoted here
as a pass; the targeted specs for this change are green and so is the other
lane's new one against it.

## Map: a quality pass — dead code, duplicated truths, and App.tsx — 2026-09-17

**One real defect.** `AudioBand` was declared identically in `features/types.ts`
and `live/audio.ts` — the same union written twice, which is exactly the second
representation of a shared truth the contributor contract forbids, and mine from
two days ago. It is defined once in the model now and imported by the device that
measures it.

**A domain expression that had been copied four times.**
`sceneCrop({ ...show.output, crop: output?.crop }, size)` was spelled out by hand
in `SurfaceCanvas`, `output.tsx`, `OutputsPanel` and `OutputProperties`. That
join is "the region this output covers"; the next change to where a region lives
would have had to find all four and would have missed one. It is `outputRegion`
now.

**Dead code.** `hasSequence` and `withScene` were exported, never called, by
anything, including tests. Removed. Twenty-three unused exports and six unused
exported types are now zero: everything used only inside its own module stopped
being exported, mine and the pre-existing alike. A wide surface is what makes a
codebase hard to change — you cannot tell what is load-bearing.

**The god file.** `App.tsx` was 1,251 lines, 12% of the source, and I had put
about 150 of them there. Three closed command sets came out, each with a single
subject and no dependency on the canvas, the panels or the output session:
`use-scene-commands.ts` (129 lines), `use-output-commands.ts`, and
`use-folder-commands.ts`. 1,251 → 1,097.

**And where I stopped, deliberately.** The rest of `App` is state declarations,
wiring and a 361-line panel layout — composition-root work. Extracting the render
would mean a component taking forty props, which is worse code wearing a smaller
line count. 1,097 lines is still big; it is big the way a composition root is big,
and I would rather say that than move the problem and call it solved.

Two things I chose not to "fix": `clamp01` exists three times, and deduplicating
a one-liner across module boundaries buys coupling for nothing — that rule is
about domain truths, not about `Math.min(1, Math.max(0, x))`. And knip reports
`vision_wasm_module_internal.js` as an unused file; it is MediaPipe's WASM
loader, fetched by URL at runtime rather than imported, and deleting it would
break hand and face tracking.

270 unit tests, 62 e2e, lint, `tsc -b` and the Map build pass, unchanged from
before the pass — which is the point of a refactor.

## Map: the four gaps that survived the parity claim — 2026-09-17

Closing "all seven gaps" was not the same as parity, and four specifics survived
the check. All four are now done.

**Kaleidoscope and tunnel.** Two of the three effects Lazy Lighting names by
name, and neither exists upstream — swirl and spiral are adjacent, not the same.
Wrapping a second shader framework to get them would have cost more than the
forty lines of GLSL each one is, so `GLShader` hosts a fragment shader on the
catalog's existing contract: `frame` in milliseconds drives it, `colors` tint it,
numeric props become uniforms of the same name. The kaleidoscope folds the circle
into mirrored wedges; the tunnel uses 1/r so equal steps crowd toward the centre,
which is what reads as depth on a flat wall. A compile or link failure throws
into the surface's existing `ShaderBoundary` rather than being swallowed, so a
GPU that cannot run them says so instead of showing a black rectangle. The
context is explicitly released on unmount — browsers cap how many live at once
and a show can hold many shader surfaces.

`features.spec.ts` already chose and rendered every effect in both the editor
and an output window; the two are in that loop now, with an added assertion that
the boundary's failure message never appears. So they are verified compiling on a
real GPU, not just typechecked.

**Face tracking.** Their copy says hand/face; Map had hands only.
`face_landmarker.task` is vendored the way the hand model already was —
committed, checksummed by `prepare-vendor.mjs`, downloaded by nothing at build
time — and the same worker loads whichever model the tracker's new `subject`
names. Only the model being watched is loaded: each is several megabytes and a
laptop driving a projector has better uses for them. A face arrives as one
landmark set, which is the shape a hand already is, so rendering, recording and
offline replay needed no changes. Switching subject drops any recording, because
a recording of hands replayed onto face landmarks is of a different thing
entirely. Absent `subject` means hands, which is what every show saved before
today meant.

**Recording resolution.** Capture arrived at the shared window's own size.
`RECORDING_SIZES` offers 720p, 1080p, 4K or the window, applied with
`applyConstraints` on the display track, and the bitrate now follows the frame
size — 12 Mbit is mush on 4K and wasteful on 720p. Constraints on a display
track are advisory, so a browser that declines still records at the window's
size rather than failing. **Stated in the UI copy:** choosing a size larger than
the window does not invent detail; for a genuine 4K master, make the output
window 4K and record at "Window".

**Library depth.** Six one-offs became fourteen scenes across four occasions —
Halloween, Christmas, Party, Ambient — several built on the two new effects and
several reacting to the bass. The picker groups them, because fourteen in a flat
list is a list you scroll rather than choose from.

270 unit tests, 62 e2e, lint, `tsc -b`, the theme-literal guard and the Map build
pass. The `features.test.ts` guard that pinned the catalog at 27 now names
Aether's own additions separately, so the upstream set still cannot lose one
silently while ours can grow.

Still true, and not closeable here: none of this has run on a projector,
a microphone, a MIDI desk, a tablet or a camera pointed at a face.

## Map: driving the new features through the real GUI — 2026-09-16

Everything built for the Lazy Lighting gaps had unit tests and no end-to-end
coverage. Two new Playwright specs drive the production build in real Chrome
against a real host, the same as the existing 56. **They found two bugs that
unit tests could not have.**

**The crossfade disagreed with the projector at full fade.** `SurfaceCanvas`
rendered the active scene's wrapper unconditionally, with `opacity ?? 1` — so
when `sceneLayers` had dropped scene A at a full fade, the editor still drew it
at full strength while the output drew only B. The viewport is supposed to be
what the projector shows; it was not. Both now render exactly what `sceneLayers`
returns, in the same order, the active layer being simply the interactive one.

**Paint dropped the brush after one stroke.** `selectSurface` resets the tool to
"select" — a one-shot draw is right for the shape tools — and the paint path
selects the surface it creates. So the first stroke landed, the tool silently
reverted, and every stroke after it was a select-drag. Node editing was already
exempt from that reset; painting is the same kind of thing, a mode you stay in,
so it is exempt now too. Found by a probe that printed the rendered stroke
geometry after each gesture: the same three points, three times.

**`performance-pipeline.spec.ts`** builds a show from the ready-made library,
engages a crossfade and checks both scenes are on screen mid-fade and one at
either end, saves, reloads and finds the fader where it was left; opens an
output and drags a surface through three passes of twenty-four pointer moves
each *while the show plays*, asserting both windows survive, the output stays
linked, and neither page threw or logged an error — the reported crash, as a
test; and gives two outputs their own scenes and regions across a reload.

**`reactive.spec.ts`** stands in for hardware this machine does not have — a
fixed spectrum for the analyser, a MIDI port the test posts into, both installed
before the app loads. It hands a shader parameter to the microphone and checks
the panel says so while the microphone is off, that the binding is document
state and the microphone is not; it moves fader 74 on the fake desk, uses
"learn", and checks a *note* message does not rebind anything; and it paints two
strokes, asserting they render on the projector as well as in the editor and
that the second joins the same painting rather than making a second layer.

62 e2e, 268 unit tests, lint, `tsc -b`, the theme-literal guard and the Map
build pass. The fakes are honest about their limit: they prove the wiring from a
device to a projected parameter, not an AnalyserNode's arithmetic or a real
desk's timing.

## Map: the remaining Lazy Lighting gaps — 2026-09-16

Gaps 2–7 from `dev/docs/roadmap/Lazy_Lighting_Parity.md`, closed in order.

**Scene crossfade.** Their standout was two channels with a live fader; we had
none. `MapShow.mix` names a B scene and a blend, and `sceneLayers` returns the
scenes on screen with the opacity each is mixed at — one entry normally, two
while a fade is engaged. A layer at zero is dropped rather than drawn invisibly,
so at either end of the fader the show costs exactly what it did before the
crossfade existed. Each scene composites into its own full-size stack before the
fader touches it, or overlapping surfaces would show through one another halfway
across. The output and the viewport both render the mix; only the active scene
is editable, because the B scene is what you are fading toward, not what you are
holding. The fader lives beside the scene list and stays on screen, because you
ride it during a show rather than setting it once. A deleted B scene collapses
the mix rather than blanking half the show.

**Video export.** `captureStream()` on the raster does not exist — the raster is
a DOM tree of images, videos, SVG and WebGL canvases, not one canvas, and
compositing it ourselves would mean a second renderer that could disagree with
the first and would get the shaders wrong. So the recorder captures the output
*window* through the browser's own screen share: what lands in the file is
exactly what the projector shows. The operator picks the window, which also
makes the capture consented rather than silent. Stopping the share from the
browser's own bar ends the recording, so the two controls cannot disagree.
**The limit:** resolution is the window's, not a chosen 4K render.

**MIDI.** Cheap, because audio had already established that a modulation has a
*source*. `live/midi.ts` keeps the latest value of every control change,
normalised; a surface names a controller the way an audio one names a band. A
fader nobody has touched reads zero rather than being absent, so a show opens
looking the same whether or not the desk is plugged in. Channels are ignored — a
fader is a fader whichever channel it speaks on — and a desk plugged in mid-show
is re-scanned rather than needing a restart. The panel offers "use the last
fader moved", because learn beats counting.

**A starting library.** Six finished scenes — Haunted fog, Pumpkin flicker,
Blood drip, Winter drift, Festive lights, Spectral swirl — each one full-bleed
surface carrying a tuned shader, several already reacting to the bass. All
generative: nothing to download, nothing to go missing from a saved show, any
resolution a projector asks for. An empty black rectangle was a bad first five
minutes; the tool was asking you to map a wall before showing you anything worth
mapping.

**Draw mode.** A `paint` tool reusing the freehand gesture exactly — it is the
same gesture; what differs is that the stroke becomes content rather than a
mask. Strokes live in the surface's own pixel space, so they warp with it as an
image would: you paint straight onto a mapped shape and the paint lands where
the shape is, not where the screen is. Strokes append to the painted surface
rather than each becoming a surface, or a minute of drawing would leave a
hundred layers in the tree. A mark needs two points where a mask needs an area,
so paint commits what the shape tools discard. The brush sits on the canvas,
where your eye already is. Brush colour and width are the operator's, not the
show's — a file records the strokes, never the brush.

**Tablet.** The canvas was already touch-driven; the furniture was not. Below
1100px the rails narrow and the input preview folds away; below 820px panels
float over the canvas rather than stealing it, and rows and controls grow to
finger size. **Phone widths are deliberately not covered:** mapping a building
through a 4-inch viewport is a different product, not a smaller stylesheet.

268 Map tests, 198 shared UI tests, lint, `tsc -b`, the theme-literal guard and
the Map, Studio, CAD and UI builds pass. No projector, microphone, MIDI desk or
tablet was available here, so each of those is verified by its logic and its
tests rather than in use.

## Map: shader parameters can follow the music — 2026-09-16

The first gap closed from `dev/docs/roadmap/Lazy_Lighting_Parity.md`. Lazy
Lighting lists audio reactivity; Map had `audio: false` in the one place it
touched a microphone. For a holiday show that is table stakes — the display is
supposed to move with what is playing.

Built as a **modulation source** rather than a system of its own, because shader
parameters already had cycles and audio is simply something else driving one.
`ShaderModulation.source` is `"time"` or `"audio"`, with a `band`.

`live/audio.ts` publishes four smoothed levels — bass, mids, treble, everything —
from an `AnalyserNode`, following the same store shape as `live/cameras.ts` so
there is one pattern for live input rather than two. Bands rather than raw FFT
bins keep the saved document independent of the analyser: a surface says "follow
the bass", not "follow bin 7", so changing the FFT size later cannot silently
retune every show ever saved. Rises are instant so a kick lands on the frame it
happens and falls are eased, because a value tracking the waveform exactly
flickers instead of pulsing. Echo cancellation, noise suppression and auto gain
are explicitly off: they are speech features and would eat the dynamics the show
is reacting to.

`modulationAt` takes the levels as an argument rather than reading the
microphone, so a show's motion stays a pure function and is testable without a
sound card — and an audio modulation carries no period, so the parser's
"zero period means off" rule had to stop applying to it.

Each window listens to its own room rather than the level crossing the channel,
which matches how each already runs its own clock. Two outputs in one room agree;
a recording of the show does not reproduce, which is inherent to reacting to a
room rather than a defect.

`shader-motion.test.ts` covers the level scaling, indifference to show time,
silence and a missing band and a dead microphone all reading as nothing, levels
outside 0..1 being clamped so a parameter cannot exceed the amount asked for, the
default band, a zero period not disabling audio, and a save/reopen round trip
keeping the band. 258 Map tests, lint, `tsc -b` and the Map build pass. No
microphone was available in this environment, so the analyser's behaviour on real
sound is reasoned from its construction, not measured.

## Map: the surface alignment pattern is a setting — 2026-09-16

A surface with no content yet paints a pattern so you can see its warp against
the real thing. That pattern is now a choice: **Grid** (lines, the existing one)
or **Checkerboard** (squares). Lines show a warp by how they bend; squares show
it by how their areas change, and which reads better depends on what you are
projecting onto.

`SurfaceGrid` gained the checkerboard beside the grid — same 8 × 7 cell count so
the two read at the same scale, same white, since this is projected light and not
interface chrome. `SurfaceMedia`'s `placeholder` went from a boolean back to a
value, now `SurfacePattern`, so the one prop says both *whether* to paint and
*which*. That is the shape an earlier attempt used to let the canvas and the
output diverge; the difference is that both now read the same field, so they
cannot.

**It lives in the document (`show.output.surfacePattern`), not in a device
preference**, which is the one real decision here. It reads like a theme, and a
theme would normally be per-browser — but the editor's viewport and every output
window have to show the same surface, and a preference stored per browser would
disagree the moment an output ran on another machine. In the document it crosses
the channel with everything else and saves with the show. Absent or unrecognised
falls back to the grid.

The setting is a Surfaces card in Map's own settings window, beside Workspace —
reachable from the suite account gear, which Map claims through
`aether-open-settings`.

`output-surface.test.tsx` covers both patterns rendering (13 lines versus 28
filled squares), the save/reopen round trip, the absent default, and a nonsense
value falling back. 256 Map tests, lint, `tsc -b`, the theme-literal guard and
the Map build pass. No projector was available, so which pattern reads better on
a wall is the point of offering both rather than something measured here.

## Map: editing during playback rebuilt the output plumbing per pointer move — 2026-09-15

Jonathan reported the tab crashing, or needing a reload, when he adjusted assets
during playback with an output window open. One root cause, in three places:
**the editor↔output plumbing was keyed on the document's value instead of on the
session.** Every edit makes a new show object, and a drag emits an edit per
pointer move, so anything listing `show` as a dependency was torn down and
rebuilt around sixty times a second for as long as the drag lasted.

**The channel.** `useOutputSession` built its `BroadcastChannel` inside an effect
depending on `show`, `transport` and `mediaUrls` — but a channel depends only on
the session. Measured: **31 channels constructed and closed for 30 pointer
moves.** Worse than the churn, each rebuild left a gap with no `onmessage`
attached, so an output's device reports could land on a closed channel and its
window go unreported while still open. The channel now lives for the session in a
ref, and a separate effect publishes the payload when it changes. The same effect
also depended on `updateDisplay`, which depended on the caller memoising its
callback — a hook whose channel lifetime hangs on a consumer's render discipline
is the same bug waiting to happen, so `onDisplay` is held by ref.

**The playhead.** `useTransport`'s animation-frame loop listed `[show, transport]`,
so an edit during playback cancelled a frame already scheduled and booked another
— once per pointer move. It reads the document and the anchor through a ref now
and restarts only on play, pause or seek.

`output-session.test.tsx` drives thirty separate commits, each its own render
rather than a batch, and pins one channel, no posts to a closed channel, all
thirty-one payloads still delivered, and nothing left open on unmount.

**The output window**, taken once the other lane's edits had been quiet for
eighteen minutes and Jonathan asked for everything fixed. Its clock had the same
`[show, transport, linked]` dependency, and two more of the same family turned up
in that file's new silence-timeout watchdog: `heardAt` was state updated on every
message, so the watchdog rebuilt its `setInterval` at pointer rate — it is never
read during render and is now a ref — and `mediaUrls ?? {}` handed the projector
a different empty object per message, re-rendering the whole tree for nothing.
The `linked` / `heardAt` feature itself is preserved.

Every "latest value" ref here is written in an effect, not during render: a
render can be discarded under concurrent rendering, and a ref written during one
would keep a value that was never committed. That also clears four `react(refs)`
warnings. 253 Map tests, lint, `tsc -b` and the Map build pass.

**Still unconfirmed:** these are defects proven by test and reading, in exactly
the reported path, but no console error was available, so whether they are *the*
crash is not claimed.

## Map: shaders gain a time model, parameter cycles, and a real panel — 2026-09-15

A shader was a preset plus a bag of numbers. It animated — `frame` has always
been driven from the show clock — but nothing about that motion could be shaped,
and its forty-odd controls were a flat stack of `FieldRow`s named after whatever
the upstream library called them.

**Time.** `ShaderTime` is `{ offsetS, loopS, direction, frozen }` and
`shaderTimeS` turns it into the seconds the effect sees. Because an effect is a
pure function of the time it is handed, shaping that time *is* its motion
control: an offset puts two surfaces on one effect out of phase instead of
pulsing together, a loop makes a seamless cycle out of an endless one, ping-pong
turns without a cut by running out and back over twice the loop, and freezing
holds a frame while the show keeps running. The editor and the projector still
agree without sharing a frame, because both compute from the same instant.

**Parameter cycles.** `ShaderModulation` adds one cycle to one numeric
parameter — `{ amount, periodS, waveform, phase }` — evaluated at the shaded
time. Keyframes would have needed a timeline per parameter; a shader's
parameters are the kind of thing you want breathing rather than choreographed,
and two numbers say that. Sine and triangle leave zero and rise so swapping
between them does not jump the value; square and ramp start at an extreme
because that is what they are. Non-numeric parameters are never modulated — a
waveform on an enum has no meaning — and an unknown parameter name is dropped
rather than invented. An unmodulated shader returns the identical object, so a
static show costs nothing per frame.

Both live in `ShaderMedia`, which the canvas, the input preview and the output
window all render through, so there is one answer everywhere rather than an
evaluation path the preview could miss.

**The panel.** Controls are now a two-column grid of icon-led fields under a
"Shader properties" heading with a reset, with the gradient colours counted
above it and sizing still folded away — an effect exposing a dozen controls was
turning into scrolling rather than reading. Labels cover the abbreviations that
do not read on their own (`focalDistance` → "Focal point distance", `grainMixer`
→ "Grain mix"); the camelCase fallback handles the rest. Icons are chosen by
*rules over the name* — colour, angle, size, rate, offset, count, light, noise,
scale, shape — not a table, because the presets between them expose about 170
distinct parameters and a table that size goes stale the first time upstream
moves. A parameter on a cycle marks its field, since the number shown is no
longer the whole truth.

`shader-motion.test.ts` covers offset including negative show time, freeze
beating a loop, wrapping, the ping-pong turn, reverse staying inside its cycle,
each waveform's range and start, phase, a zero period being off rather than a
divide by zero, modulation skipping non-numeric and unknown parameters, the
identity return, and a save/reopen round trip that drops a zero-period cycle and
falls back on an unknown direction.

248 Map tests, 198 shared UI tests, the theme-literal guard, lint, `tsc -b` and
the Map and UI builds pass. No browser was available, so the panel's layout is
verified through its markup and types rather than seen.

## Map: square new surfaces, and a shader picker you can scan — 2026-09-15

**New surfaces start square.** `newSurface` insetted the scene box by 20% on each
side, so on a 1920×1080 scene every new surface began 1488×648 — the artboard's
aspect, not a shape anyone chose. They are now a centred square of 60% of the
scene's short edge, still cascading by index so a second one does not land exactly
on the first, and the source box matches the quad. A surface therefore opens with
square grid cells and undistorted content: the first thing you do is warp it onto
the wall, not un-stretch the artboard. This covers shaders too — every feature
kind is built on `newSurface`.

**The shader default was already right**, and is now pinned rather than assumed:
`newFeature("shader", …)` starts on `mesh-gradient` with `speed: 1`, and `speed`
scales the `frame` that `ShaderMedia` drives from the show clock, so it animates
as the show plays. Its colours come from the upstream preset and nothing lands in
the media store — a shader is a recipe, not an asset.

**The picker is sectioned.** Twenty-seven effects is past the point where a flat
`<select>` is read rather than scanned. `SHADER_SECTIONS` groups them by what they
do on a surface — Gradients, Noise & organic, Motion & fluid, Patterns & dots,
Light & texture — and the seven that transform an assigned picture rather than
generating one now carry an image marker in the list and on the trigger, because
choosing one with no media assigned is a half-made surface.

That needed one shared addition: `MenuItem.heading`. `separatorBefore` divides a
menu but does not say what into, which is fine for six commands and not for
twenty-seven effects. It renders above the item as a small caps label, and the
shader picker is a `MenuButton` rather than a `SelectField` because a native
option cannot carry the image icon. The trigger is styled to line up with the
selects it sits beside in the properties panel.

242 Map tests, 198 shared UI tests, the theme-literal guard, lint, `tsc -b` and
the Map, UI, CAD, Studio and Animation builds pass.

## Map: the viewport renders what the projector renders — 2026-09-15

Same day, correcting the entry below it. Making the output paint empty surfaces
was right; giving it a *different* picture from the editor was not. The canvas
drew `.map-checker` and the output drew `TestPattern` — a circle, diagonals and
an "Aether Map" caption — so the two disagreed about the same surface, and the
canvas stopped being a preview of anything.

There is now one placeholder, one look, one flag. `SurfaceMedia`'s `placeholder`
is a boolean again; the canvas, the input preview and a live output all pass it
and all get `.map-surface-grid`. What the output legitimately drops is editor
chrome — the setup photo, outlines, handles — not surface content.

**It is a grid, not a checkerboard.** Straight lines are the only thing that
reveals how a mapping warps, which is exactly what you are judging while dragging
corners onto a physical contour; a checkerboard shows the warp only at its
corners. The lines are white rather than themed because on a wall they are light,
not interface chrome — `.map-checker`'s two near-black interface greys were
invisible projected. Cells are a fixed count (8 × 7) rather than a fixed pixel
size, so a surface covering a whole wall and one covering a window pane show the
same readable grid.

The line weight has to be proportional too, and a first pass in CSS got this
wrong: the element a surface paints into is its *source* box, often 1920 wide,
warped down to a few hundred screen pixels, so a 1px line rendered at about an
eighth of a pixel and washed out to nothing. `SurfaceGrid` draws it as SVG with a
stroke of 0.9% of the surface's long edge — even on both axes, which a
percentage-tiled CSS background cannot be on a non-square surface, and identical
in the editor and on the projector. `output-surface.test.tsx` pins the
proportional stroke and the cell count so it cannot silently return to hairlines. The old full test pattern stays what it always was: a
whole-output calibration image, still reachable as a surface's explicit source
and as `output.testPattern`.

**A projection surface has its own icon.** `core/assets/icons/surface-map.svg`
is the existing warped-quad outline with a perspective grid inside it, following
the same vanishing lines. Map's layer rows, its Surfaces filter and the New
Surface command use it, so the thing and its picture agree. The plain `surface`
quad icon stays for anything that means the shape rather than the mapping.

The rectangular projection surface itself is intact and is still the default:
`newFeature("surface", …)` builds a plain quad with no source, which is what the
ribbon's New Surface creates.

239 Map tests, 198 shared UI tests, the theme-literal guard, lint, `tsc -b` and
the Map and UI builds pass. No projector was available, so the grid's legibility
on a wall is reasoned from its contrast, not measured.

## Map: an empty surface now paints on the output — 2026-09-15

The output window rendered nothing for a surface with no media assigned. Only the
editor canvas passed `placeholder` to `SurfaceMedia`; `OutputSurface` never did,
so `SurfaceMedia` returned `null` and the projector stayed black no matter how
many surfaces the scene held.

That is the wrong end to be empty. Matching a projection to a physical contour is
done by looking at the projected shape on the real object and dragging corners
until they line up — you cannot align what does not emit light. An empty surface
is precisely the state you are in while doing it.

An output fed by a live editor session now paints empty surfaces. A deployed show
does not: no editor is driving it, and a placeholder there would land on the
building itself mid-performance.

**And it paints the alignment grid, not the editor's checkerboard.** `.map-checker`
is drawn from `--aether-color-bg-hover` over `--aether-color-bg-app` — in dark
mode `#23262b` on `#0e1013`, two near-blacks. Correct in the editor, invisible
projected onto a wall in a dark room, which is the only place it would have been
seen. `SurfaceMedia`'s `placeholder` is now `"checker" | "alignment"` instead of a
boolean: the editor canvas and input preview ask for the checkerboard, the live
output asks for `TestPattern`'s grid — white lines, a circle and diagonals, the
pattern already built in this repo for judging warp and keystone.

`output-surface.test.tsx` covers the grid on a live output, the checkerboard not
substituting for it, a deployed show painting neither, and a hidden or fully
transparent surface painting nothing either way. 239 Map tests, lint, `tsc -b`
and the Map build pass. No projector was available, so the grid's legibility on a
wall is reasoned from its contrast, not measured.

## Map: one Outputs card, with the device as a property — 2026-09-15

Outputs and Devices were two cards in the same rail describing the same thing
from opposite ends: one listed where the show plays, the other chose what it
plays on, and nothing connected them. A `DevicesPanel` segmented control picked
"Monitor / Edge device / Wireless" in local state that no output ever saw.

They are now one card. `ShowOutput.kind` gained `"edge"` and a `deviceId`, so the
device an output plays on is a property of that output — which transport, and for
an edge output which paired player — read and written where every other property
of it lives. `DevicesPanel` is gone, split along the line its two halves already
followed:

- `OutputProperties` (right rail, "Output") — the selected output's device type,
  its monitor/wireless/edge specifics, the scene it shows and the region it
  covers. This absorbs `OutputCropPanel`.
- `DeviceManager` — pairing, naming, forgetting and deploying to the workspace's
  players. That is about hardware, not about any one output, so it is a tool of
  the collection: a **Devices** button in the Outputs tray beside New output,
  opening a dialog. Opening an edge output opens it too, since an edge output has
  no window here — its player runs the show on the projector, and "open" means
  deploy.

**Each row says what it is actually reaching.** `outputConnection` gives every
row the same link icon on two different truths: a window output is live while its
window is open; an edge output is live while its player is checked in *and*
playing this show — an online player running something else is not this output's
picture, and a row that claimed otherwise would be lying at exactly the moment it
matters. An edge output with no device chosen shows no link at all rather than a
broken one. It lives in `output-connection.ts`, not in the panel: the panel file
drags in the host API, and this rule deserves a test that does not need a DOM.

`useMapDevices` replaces the polling `DevicesPanel` held privately, so the tree
and the manager agree about what is online instead of polling on separate clocks.

`outputs.test.ts` adds the connection matrix: window open and closed, player
online-and-playing, offline, online-but-on-another-show, unassigned, no device
chosen, and that an open window never makes an edge output live. 236 Map tests,
lint, `tsc -b` and the Map build pass. No browser was available, so the merged
card is verified through its logic and types rather than seen.

## Map: outputs are a list, and they live in the left rail — 2026-09-15

`show.output` was one object: one region, one device, one everything. A projection
show that drives two projectors and a lobby screen had nowhere to say so. Outputs
are now `show.outputs: ShowOutput[]` — `{ id, name, kind, sceneId?, crop? }` —
and each one is a device the show plays to, with its own region and, optionally,
its own scene.

**Scene binding reuses the active scene rather than threading a parameter.**
`showForOutput(show, output)` returns the show with `activeSceneId` rebound to
that output's scene, so `evaluateShow`, `sceneSize` and `activeSurfaces` need no
notion of which output is asking: one window's scene is simply the active scene,
from its own view. An output naming a scene that no longer exists falls back to
the active one on read — deleting a scene must not silently dark a projector.

**Windows are keyed by output id, not by transport.** `useOutputSession` already
held a map of open windows, keyed by `"monitor"` / `"cast"` / `"airplay"`; that
key was the thing preventing two projectors. It is now the output id, the window
name is too (so reopening an output reuses its window instead of stacking a
second on the same projector), and the device report carries `outputID`, so the
editor knows which output reported which size. `onDisplay` hands back a record of
every open window rather than one "current" display, and `closeOutput` was added
so the tree can close what it opened.

**`MapShow.output` stays**, holding the show-level raster size and the two panic
controls. Blackout and the test grid are deliberately global: a blackout is never
per-device.

**Migration.** A file written before outputs were a list gets one output carrying
its old `output.crop`, so it opens with the projector it was authored for. A show
always has at least one output — with none there is nothing to open a window on.

**The rail.** Outputs are a third tree in the left rail beside Scenes and Layers,
on the shared `TreePanel`, and Devices moved left to join them. The left rail is
what the show contains; the right rail is properties of what is selected, and an
output is a thing in the show, not a property of a selection.

Outputs are deliberately **not** rows in the Layers tree. A layer paints — it has
z-order, opacity, visibility, lock, animation and folders. An output is a viewport
onto a scene, not content within one, and every layer command would have needed a
special case for it (what does "move output forward" mean? what does dragging one
into a folder do?). The backdrop already costs `LayersPanel` a scatter of
`if (background?.id === id)` branches; a second pseudo-layer would double that.
Each output row instead carries read-only child rows for its scene and region,
shows its live size while a window is open, and dims when none is.

`outputs.test.ts` covers the migration of a legacy file, the always-one-output
guarantee, a two-output round trip keeping separate scenes and regions, per-output
scene sizing through the rebind, the deleted-scene fallback, and `findOutput`
answering for a window that names nothing so a deployed device still plays. 235
Map tests, lint, `tsc -b` and the Map build pass.

Not done: the canvas draws only the selected output's region, so overlapping
regions from several outputs are not shown at once. `OutputDialog` and
`DevicesPanel` still act on the selected output rather than offering a picker.

## Map: an unconfigured output shows the whole scene — 2026-09-15

`sceneCrop` returned `fit: "cover"` when a show had no output region saved, and
`output.tsx` corrected that to `"contain"` only for a wireless session. A monitor
output window therefore scaled the scene to *fill* the window and cut whatever
did not fit: a 1920×1080 scene in a 960×508 window rendered at 960×540 and lost
16px off the top and bottom before anyone had chosen to crop anything. Two
transports also disagreed about the same unconfigured show for no reason.

The default is now `"contain"` in `sceneCrop` itself, so every consumer — monitor
window, wireless, deployed layout, editor preview — shows an unconfigured output
the whole scene, letterboxed. Cropping is a choice you make, not a default you
discover. A saved region is still honoured exactly as written, `cover` included.
The wireless special case in `output.tsx` is gone.

This also closes a hole opened by the canvas output region the same day: seeding a
region by dragging the new overlay would have stamped the old `"cover"` default
into the show, silently changing how the output fitted on first touch.

`crop-snap.test.ts` pins the whole-scene default, its transform, the `cover`
behaviour it replaces, and that an explicit saved fit survives. 230 Map tests and
the Map build pass.

## Map: the scene is a boundary, and the output window is a region on it — 2026-09-15

**A scene now shows only what it projects.** Surfaces were already clipped to the
scene box — `.map-surface` is scene-sized with `overflow: hidden` — but the setup
photo was not: `.map-setup-background` sizes to the image, which is normally far
larger than the scene, so it spilled across the canvas as loose pixels that would
never reach a projector. It is now wrapped in a scene-sized clip box.

The clip lifts for whichever layer is selected, photo included. That is the point
of the boundary rather than a contradiction of it: while you are positioning a
layer you need to see the part hanging outside, and once you deselect it the scene
tells the truth about what gets projected again. The same `data-unclipped` rule
covers ordinary surfaces, so a layer dragged half off the scene reads the same way.

**The output window is drawn on the scene.** The crop region existed in the model
and had a numeric panel, but the canvas only drew it once a crop had already been
saved — so the region you were projecting was invisible at the moment you most
needed it. `SurfaceCanvas` takes the open output window (`outputDevice`) and draws
the region whenever one is open, defaulting to the whole scene, so opening an
output window immediately shows what it covers.

The overlay now behaves like a sketch artboard: four corner handles that resize
from the opposite corner, a drag to move, and everything outside the region dimmed
through one even-odd path — when the region is the whole scene the cut-out is the
scene and nothing dims. Dragging latches to the scene's four corners, four edge
midpoints and centre, which fall out of offering each axis its leading edge,
centre and trailing edge (`crop-snap.ts`). The tolerance is 7 screen pixels
converted through the zoom, so the latch feels identical at every scale instead of
snapping across half the scene when zoomed out. Snapping honours the canvas's Snap
toggle and Alt-to-bypass, the same convention as layer dragging. Nothing is
clamped to the scene: a projector may legitimately overscan.

`crop-snap.test.ts` covers the anchors, the nearest-anchor rule, the
outside-tolerance no-op, an exact hit at zero tolerance, and that a region dragged
past its own origin keeps a positive size. `SurfaceCanvas.test.tsx` covers the
clip and its selected exemption for both the photo and ordinary layers, the region
appearing on an open output window with no crop saved, its four handles, and a
drag latching to centre with Alt bypassing it. 229 Map tests and the Map build
pass. No browser was available, so the dimming and cursors are asserted through
the DOM rather than seen.

## Map layer folders, and a footer button that stopped moving — 2026-09-15

**The overflow button jumped when you opened it.** `CollectionFooter` rendered
its open menu inside a wrapper `<div>`, a sibling of the buttons in a
`justify-content: space-between` flex row. The menu itself is `position: fixed`
and takes no space, but the wrapper was still a flex item, so opening the menu
gave the row three items instead of two and space-between shifted the button
under the pointer. The wrapper is gone; the menu renders directly.

**Map layers have folders.** The shared tray's New folder command was inert here
— Map had no folders to wire it to. It does now.

A folder is a name a layer carries (`Surface.folder`), not a registry: it exists
exactly while some layer names it, so there is nothing to keep in sync and no
empty folder to collect. Array order is paint order, so a folder has to be one
contiguous run or the tree would claim a z-order the renderer does not have.
`groupSurfaces` restores that invariant after every change and on read — each
folder's run sits where its first member sat, members keep their relative order,
and loose layers keep their own positions, so folders and loose layers still
interleave. It is idempotent, and `parseShow` applies it, so a hand-edited or
older file opens grouped.

Forming a folder, or leaving one, keeps a layer exactly where it paints —
grouping must never silently change what covers what. Joining an existing folder
puts the layer at the top of that run, which is what dropping onto a folder row
means. Dragging beside another layer adopts that layer's folder, so one gesture
both reorders and moves a layer in or out. Locked layers refuse both. Renaming a
folder row renames it on every member; dissolving keeps the layers and their
order and drops only the grouping. The footer's New folder button groups the
selected layer and opens the new row for rename; the row context menu carries
Move to new folder, Move to each existing folder, and Move out.

`Surface.folder` is an optional field on the existing version 2 — no bump: a
reader that does not know it ignores it and loses only the grouping, and Map is
the only reader. `layer-folders.test.ts` covers the contiguity invariant and its
idempotence, in/between/out moves, the locked refusal, drop-beside adoption,
rename, dissolve, name allocation, and a save/reopen round trip including the
regrouping of a file whose runs were broken.

Folder rows are tree-only and do not themselves drag — moving a whole folder is
not wired. 222 Map tests, 198 shared UI tests, and the Map, UI, CAD, Studio and
Animation builds pass. No browser was available, so the drag gestures are
covered by their helpers' tests rather than by a live drag.

Map Scenes, Animation Parts/Mates/Clips and the CAD Drawing panel still show the
shared tray's New folder button disabled; each needs its own product decision
about what a folder means there.

## Studio navigation: the suite sidebar, not a collection tree — 2026-09-15

Studio's own shell navigated with `ListBox` — a collection control, which pulls
in `.aui-collection`'s tree presentation: option rows, tree geometry, the
collection's chrome. The suite already has the right frame for this and every
app home page uses it: `CollapsibleSidebar`, which the settings shell was the
only navigation surface not using. The practical cost was that Studio's sidebar
could not collapse, on the one screen where a 250px rail is most often in the
way.

The `<aside>` is now a `CollapsibleSidebar` (`id="studio-nav"`, `toggle="custom"`)
and the `ListBox` is a `<nav>` of plain rows: icon, `SidebarLabel`, optional
badge. Rows, rail width, hover and the collapse preference come from
`.aui-sidebar`'s constant-geometry contract, so icons hold their exact position
between states; the collapse toggle sits in the workspace identity row beside the
Studio mark, matching the library homes. Studio keeps its own width, gradient,
identity block and accent-filled current row.

Collapsed, the header becomes a divider and search, host label and Sign out drop
out — none has a one-icon form — leaving the workspace mark, the navigation
icons and the profile avatar. The 640px rule that narrows the sidebar to 155px
still applies while expanded; the rail out-specifies it, as that contract's
doubled-class comment intends.

`.studio-sidebar`'s `.aui-listbox` and `[role="option"]` overrides are gone.
Theme-literal check, typecheck and the Studio build pass, and 198 shared UI tests
still pass. Studio has no test harness of its own and no browser was available,
so the collapsed rail is verified by the contract it now shares with the app
homes, not by a rendered measurement.

## Collection tree: no second card, and a fixed folder command — 2026-09-15

`.aui-collection` — the shared surface under every authoring tree (CAD Items and
Mates, Map Layers and Scenes, Animation Parts/Mates/Clips, the Drawing panel) —
was drawing a card of its own: a 3px margin, an accent-tinted 1px border, an 11px
radius, and a fill of `--aether-color-bg-panel` mixed 9% toward the text colour.
Hosted inside a panel that already is a card, that read as a box inside a box,
and the fill was visibly darker than every other card in the suite (light mode:
about `#e6e6e8` against `#fbfbfc`).

It now draws none of that. The collection is transparent and borderless; the
panel hosting it is the card. Only the controls inside it stay tinted —
`--collection-control` (the filter chip, footer hovers) now derives from
`--aether-color-bg-panel` directly, since there is no longer a collection fill to
derive from. `--collection-bg` is gone.

**New folder is the footer's fixed first command.** The tray used to show
whichever control matched `^(new|add|create|folder)` first, so it was a folder in
CAD Items and a new-surface glyph in Map Layers — the tray read differently in
every panel. It now always leads with a `folder-add` button, then the product's
own new/add command, then the overflow menu. A collection whose data has no
folders still shows the button, disabled, with a title saying so; wiring a
control whose id contains "folder" claims it. Map Layers, Scenes, Parts, Mates
and Clips show the disabled form until those products add folders.

The disclosure chevron needed no change: `Tree` has always rendered one for any
row with children (or with a loading/errored branch), and the reference panels in
the screenshots simply held flat data. `TreePanel.test.tsx` now pins both — the
footer's exact button order and the chevron's presence on a branch and absence on
its leaves — so neither can regress silently.
